paragraphs.text: Retinitis pigmentosa-56 is an autosomal recessive retinal dystrophy caused by mutation in the IMPG2 gene, which encodes interphotoreceptor matrix proteoglycan-2. Bandah-Rozenfeld et al. (2010) reported that most affected individuals had early-onset retinitis pigmentosa with progressive visual field loss and deterioration of visual acuity.

paragraphs.text: Bandah-Rozenfeld et al. (2010) studied 2 families with retinitis pigmentosa, each with 3 affected sibs: one family was of Iraqi Jewish ancestry and the other was Dutch. They also studied 10 additional index cases of Dutch, Israeli, Italian, and Pakistani origin. Most patients with IMPG2 mutations had an early-onset form of retinitis pigmentosa with progressive visual field loss and deterioration of visual acuity. One patient, who carried a missense mutation, was instead diagnosed with maculopathy.

paragraphs.text: Bandah-Rozenfeld et al. (2010) sequenced the IMPG2 gene in the index cases of 2 families with autosomal recessive retinitis pigmentosa, each with 3 affected sibs. They found homozygous mutations that cosegregated with the disease in each family. The 3 affected sibs of Iraqi Jewish ancestry carried a homozygous nonsense mutation. The 3 affected sibs in the Dutch family carried a homozygous 1.8-kb genomic deletion that removes exon 9 and results in the absence of 7 amino acids in a conserved SEA domain of the IMPG2 protein. In transiently transfected COS-1 cells, a construct expressing the wildtype IMPG2 SEA domain was targeted to the plasma membrane. In contrast, the mutant construct lacking the 7 amino acids appeared to be retained in the endoplasmic reticulum.

paragraphs.text: Bandah-Rozenfeld et al. (2010) studied a Dutch family in which 3 sibs had autosomal recessive retinitis pigmentosa. In the affected sibs they identified a homozygous 1.8-kb genomic deletion in the IMPG2 gene that removes exon 9 and results in the absence of 7 amino acids in a conserved SEA domain of the protein. The deletion cosegregated with the disease in the family. In transiently transfected COS-1 cells, the wildtype SEA domain construct was targeted to the plasma membrane, whereas the mutant construct lacking the 7 amino acids appeared to be retained in the endoplasmic reticulum.
